title: Biliary Strictures
subject: Medicine
summary: Biliary strictures are abnormal narrowings of the extra‑hepatic or intra‑hepatic bile ducts, most often caused by stones, inflammation, or malignancy. They present with jaundice, pruritus, and abdominal pain, and require imaging and, if possible, ERCP or surgery. Early recognition prevents liver failure and cholangiocarcinoma.

sections.p: A biliary stricture is a focal narrowing of a bile duct that impedes flow of bile from the liver to the duodenum. Diagnosis is based on clinical features and imaging that shows a tapered segment with upstream dilatation.
b: Jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools

t.b: Shows upstream ductal dilatation and a focal narrowing – confirms obstruction but not cause
Non‑invasive imaging of the biliary tree; identifies strictures, stones, and masses
Diagnostic and therapeutic; allows brush cytology, stenting, and stone removal
Total >34 µmol/L (2 mg/dL) suggests significant obstruction; rising trend indicates worsening
>2× upper limit indicates cholestasis; helps differentiate hepatic vs. extrahepatic causes

sections.p: Strictures are staged by length, degree of narrowing, and associated complications. The Bismuth classification is used for hilar strictures, while distal strictures are graded by the length of the narrowed segment.
b: Bismuth I–IV for hilar strictures; I = <1 cm, IV = involves both ducts

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the hierarchy of causes reflects local disease burden.
b: Chronic cholecystitis leading to post‑cholecystectomy stricture

sections.p: Patients often report a triad of jaundice, pruritus, and abdominal pain. Weight loss and anorexia may signal malignancy.
b: Right upper quadrant pain, especially after fatty meals

sections.p: Start with inexpensive tests; advance to imaging if available.

t.b: Rule out anemia or infection; leukocytosis may suggest cholangitis
Elevated ALP and GGT with normal transaminases indicates cholestasis
Elevated in autoimmune pancreatitis causing stricture
First‑line imaging; shows dilated ducts and possible stones
Preferred when available; delineates anatomy and rule out malignancy
Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment of malignant strictures

sections.p: Urgent referral is required for signs of acute cholangitis or impending liver failure.
b: Fever, chills, right upper quadrant tenderness (Charcot’s triad) – acute cholangitis

t.b: Indicates severe obstruction; risk of hepatic encephalopathy
Coagulopathy from liver dysfunction; increases surgical risk

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve obstruction, and monitor liver function.
b: Endoscopic stenting for benign strictures or palliation of malignancy

t.b: Relieves obstruction; chosen over surgery when anatomy is difficult or patient is unfit for surgery
Used for cholangitis; avoid nephrotoxic drugs in renal impairment
Reduces pruritus by binding bile acids; avoid in severe liver failure

sections.p: Regular imaging and liver function tests are needed to detect recurrence or progression.
b: MRCP every 6–12 months for malignant strictures

sections.p: Conditions that mimic biliary strictures include gallstones, hepatic abscess, and pancreatic pseudocyst.
Normal bilirubin can occur early; ALP may be normal in small strictures; imaging may miss short strictures.
b: Early cholestasis may have normal LFTs; repeat testing if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Fever with RUQ pain (acute cholangitis), sudden worsening jaundice, signs of hepatic encephalopathy, or bleeding from varices

faq.q: What is the most common cause of biliary strictures in East Africa?
faq.a: Choledocholithiasis secondary to gallstone disease is the most frequent cause.

faq.q: Can a biliary stricture be asymptomatic?
faq.a: Yes, short or mild strictures may be silent until they cause obstruction or complications.

faq.q: Why is ERCP preferred over surgery in many cases?
faq.a: ERCP is less invasive, allows simultaneous diagnosis and treatment, and is safer in patients with comorbidities.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man presents with jaundice and RUQ pain. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a focal narrowing. What is the next best step? — ERCP for diagnosis and possible stenting.
A patient with a known pancreatic head tumour develops worsening jaundice. Which imaging modality best defines the extent of biliary involvement? — MRCP.
A child in a malaria-endemic area has painless jaundice. What infectious cause should be considered? — Tuberculous cholangitis or schistosomiasis.
You find a 2‑cm stricture at the hepatic hilum. According to Bismuth classification, what type is this? — Type I.
A patient with a biliary stricture is started on antibiotics for cholangitis. Which drug should be avoided in renal failure? — Nephrotoxic antibiotics such as aminoglycosides.
A patient has a biliary stricture and pruritus unresponsive to cholestyramine. What is the next therapeutic option? — Endoscopic stenting or percutaneous drainage.
